name: Bonapartism
description: The early Napoleonic tradition of central executive authority, plebiscitary legitimacy, civil equality and protected property. This profile covers its First Empire foundations, rather than every later Bonapartist movement.
scope: The political principles of the early Napoleonic settlement: executive and dynastic authority claiming national delegation, uniform civil law, property rights, state administration and national power. Bonapartism developed as a named movement after 1815; later liberal-imperial and social programmes are not projected backwards.
phrase: A society united by a strong national executive, supported through public ratification, that maintains civil equality, secure property and an orderly state.

sources.title: Le Code Civil: naissance, principes et postérité
Was the Napoleonic regime a military dictatorship?

axes: Executive power claims national delegation through ratification, not a parliamentary right to direct or dismiss the emperor. Appointed administration and controlled legislatures are central.
Plebiscites and civil legal institutions qualify personal power; neither establishes competitive elections or citizen-initiated legislation. The named movement was later elaborated.

Uniform civil institutions and a shared national political community coexist with accommodation of recognised confessions. Civil incorporation does not imply equal recognition of all cultural practices.
The civil code is non-confessional; cultural uniformity is not an inference from private Catholic belief. Overseas exclusion and restored slavery limit universal claims.

National administration regulates entry and allegiance; incorporation of useful foreigners is possible within sovereign civil authority. The doctrine is not a general open-borders programme.
Specific annual caps, sponsorship and university pathways have no direct early nineteenth-century equivalent. Responses are qualified translations of sovereignty and ordered incorporation.

An active foreign policy, national prestige and military capacity are characteristic early Napoleonic aims. These principles do not turn civilian executive rule into military rule.
Diplomacy and legal civilian authority remain important. Autonomous weapons and modern service arrangements are analogies, not recorded proposals.

Private property does not settle every modern utility or hospital question; strategic exceptions and cost conditions require independent treatment.

Civil equality secures property and inheritance rather than equalising material outcomes. Public relief and national service obligations coexist with low redistributive ambition.
Equality before civil law is not equal income. A modest safety floor may serve order without large wealth transfers; modern tax instruments remain inferred.
